sentences: A New Summer Morning
Summer vacation is here!
Yesterday was the last day of school, and today is the first day of my long vacation.
I don't need to get up at six anymore, but I still get up early.
Why?
Because my mom has a rule: in our house, everyone gets up before eight, even in summer.
This morning, I got up at seven thirty.
I brushed my teeth, washed my face, and ate breakfast with my family.
We had eggs, toast, and milk.
Dad said, "Don't be lazy this summer.
Early birds have more time to play!" I think he is right.
When I get up early, the morning feels long and cool, and I can finish my homework before lunch.
Then I have the whole afternoon to play.
What a great start to summer!
My Favorite Room
My home is not big, but I love every room in it.
The living room has a soft sofa and a big window.
The kitchen always smells good because Mom loves cooking.
But my favorite room is my bedroom.
My bedroom is small.
There is a bed, a desk, and a bookshelf.
Last month, my room was very messy.
There were books on the floor and clothes on the chair.
I couldn't find my favorite comic book!
So I made a change.
Now I clean my room every Sunday.
I put my books on the shelf and my clothes in the closet.
A clean room feels comfortable.
Now I like to read and draw in my bedroom.
It is small, but it is the best place in the world to me.
Helping at Home
During summer vacation, everyone in my family has a job at home.
Mom cooks the meals.
Dad washes the dishes after dinner.
My little sister feeds the cat and waters the plants.
And me?
I sweep the floor and take out the trash.
At first, I didn't like my jobs.
Sweeping the floor is boring, and the trash is smelly!
But then Mom told me, "When we all help a little, nobody has to work a lot." Now I understand.
Mom is busy, and our help makes her smile.
Last night, we finished the housework in twenty minutes because everyone helped.
After that, we ate watermelon and watched a movie together in the living room.
Helping at home is not so bad.
It makes our family time longer and happier.
A Big Family Dinner
Last Saturday, we had a big family dinner at my grandparents' house.
My aunt, my uncle, and my three cousins all came.
There were twelve people in the house!
Grandma cooked all afternoon.
She made chicken soup, fish, and fried noodles.
My aunt brought her famous dumplings.
Everyone says her dumplings are the best in the family.
My cousins and I set the table and helped carry the dishes.
At dinner, the adults chatted about work and the summer weather.
We kids talked about our vacation plans.
My cousin Kevin wants to learn swimming.
I told him about my plan to read ten books this summer.
He laughed and said, "Ten books?
You can do it!" After dinner, we ate mango ice together.
I love big family dinners.
The food is great, but being together is even better.
Busy Dad, Free Dad
My dad is a very busy man.
On weekdays, he gets up at six, drives to work, and comes home after seven in the evening.
Sometimes he still answers phone calls at night.
I often see him yawn at dinner.
But on the weekend, Dad becomes a different person.
He is free!
On Saturday mornings, he sleeps until nine.
Then he makes a big brunch for us.
In the afternoon, he plays basketball with me in the park, and we always buy a cold drink after the game.
Last night I asked him, "Dad, are you tired of your busy life?" He smiled and said, "I work hard on weekdays, so I can enjoy my free time with you on weekends.
That's my favorite habit." I hope I can be like Dad — work hard, play hard, and always have time for family.
A Good Night's Sleep
Do you sleep well at night?
Last week, I didn't.
Every night, I played games on my phone in bed.
I told myself, "Just ten more minutes." But the ten minutes always became one hour!
I went to sleep after midnight and got up at noon.
I felt tired all day, and my eyes hurt.
Mom saw the problem.
She made a new rule: no phones in the bedroom after ten.
At first, I thought the rule was terrible.
But something interesting happened.
Without my phone, I took a warm shower, read a book, and fell asleep quickly.
I slept for nine hours and had a sweet dream.
Now I feel fresh in the morning.
My eyes don't hurt anymore.
Good sleep is like a superpower — it makes everything better.
Maybe Mom's rules are not so bad after all.
Sunday, Our Family Day
In my family, Sunday is "Family Day." It is our weekly habit.
We don't make other plans on Sunday.
We just spend the day together.
This morning, we got up late and made pancakes together.
Dad flipped the pancakes high in the air, and one almost hit the ceiling!
We laughed so hard.
After breakfast, we cleaned the house together.
With four people working, it took only thirty minutes.
In the afternoon, we walked to the park near our home.
Mom and Dad chatted under a big tree.
My sister and I shared an ice cream and fed the fish in the pond.
Before dinner, we called Grandma and chatted with her for an hour.
My classmates say Family Day sounds boring.
I don't think so.
A simple day together makes everyone happy.
It is the warmest part of my week.
The Hungry Afternoon
Yesterday afternoon, my cousin and I rode our bikes to the sports park.
We played badminton for two hours under the hot sun.
When we stopped, we were hungry and thirsty.
"I can eat a horse!" my cousin said.
We looked in our pockets.
We only had fifty dollars together.
What could we buy?
Near the park, there was a small shop.
We bought one big bottle of water and shared it first.
Then we bought two tea eggs and a bag of crackers.
We sat under a tree and ate our little snack slowly.
"This is the best snack in the world," my cousin said with a big smile.
I laughed.
When you are really hungry, even simple food tastes amazing.
We rode home slowly and had a big dinner that night.
Grandpa's Vegetable Garden
My grandpa has a small vegetable garden behind his house.
He grows tomatoes, cucumbers, and sweet corn.
He also keeps five hens, so we always have fresh eggs.
This morning, I helped Grandpa in the garden.
We picked ten red tomatoes and three big cucumbers.
The tomatoes smelled like sunshine.
Grandpa said, "Vegetables from your own garden always taste better.
Do you know why?" I shook my head.
He smiled and said, "Because you water them and wait for them.
The waiting makes them sweet." At lunch, Grandma cooked rice with our fresh vegetables and eggs.
It was a simple meal, but everything tasted wonderful.
Grandpa is right.
Food is not just about eating.
It is also about time, care, and love.
Dinner at a Restaurant
Last night was Mom's birthday, so we went to a restaurant for dinner.
It is a popular place, and we waited fifteen minutes for our seats.
The waiter gave us the menu and some warm tea.
There were so many dishes!
Dad let me order for everyone.
I was a little nervous, but I did it.
"We would like one fish, one chicken soup, two vegetable dishes, and four bowls of rice, please," I said.
The waiter smiled and said, "Good choice!" The food came fast, and everything was delicious.
Mom loved the fish the most.
We sang a birthday song, and the restaurant gave Mom a small cake for free.
When Dad paid the bill, he said, "Good job tonight.
Next time, you can order in English!" Ha!
Maybe I need more practice first.
Sweet, Sour, and Spicy
My family has a funny game at dinner.
We call it "One New Taste." Every Thursday, we try one food we have never eaten before.
Last Thursday, Dad brought home some green sauce from India.
It looked strange, but it smelled fresh, like lemon and mint.
Mom tried it first.
"It's sour!" she said.
My sister tried it and shouted, "No, it's spicy!" Then I tried it with some bread.
It was sour, spicy, and a little sweet — all at the same time!
Dad laughed at our faces.
"Food is like a small trip," he said.
"You can taste another country without leaving home." I agree with him.
Some new foods are strange, and some are delicious.
But trying them is always fun.
Next Thursday, we will try cheese from France.
I can't wait!
Night at the Market
On Friday night, my aunt took my cousin and me to the night market.
The sky was dark, but the market was bright and loud.
The air smelled like fried chicken and sweet cakes.
The most popular stand sold fried squid.
There was a long line of customers, maybe thirty people!
"Is it really that good?" I asked.
My cousin nodded.
"It's cheap and delicious.
Trust me." We waited twenty minutes.
When I finally took a bite, I understood.
It was crispy outside and soft inside.
Amazing!
After that, we drank papaya milk and played a ring toss game.
My cousin won a small toy duck.
My aunt bought fresh fruit to take home.
On the bus home, my feet were tired, but my stomach was happy.
I love night market nights.
Cooking with Mom
It rained all day today, so we stayed home.
In the afternoon, Mom asked me, "Do you want to learn to make egg fried rice?" Of course I said yes!
First, Mom taught me how to cut green onions.
"Slowly," she said.
"Keep your fingers safe." Then I mixed two eggs in a bowl.
Mom heated the pan, and I poured the eggs in.
The kitchen was full of a wonderful smell.
Next came the rice.
Mom said the secret is to use cold rice from yesterday.
We mixed the rice and eggs together and added a little salt.
I tasted it.
"It needs more salt," I said, just like a real cook!
At dinner, everyone ate my fried rice.
Dad said it was better than his.
That made me so proud.
Cooking is hard work, but sharing your food is the best feeling.
Eat Smart, Feel Great
Do you love fried chicken and bubble tea?
Me too!
But last month, I ate junk food almost every day.
I felt tired, and I couldn't run fast in PE class.
My body was telling me something: "Please eat better!" So my sister and I made three simple rules.
Rule one: eat fruit or vegetables at every meal.
Rule two: drink water first when we are thirsty, not sweet drinks.
Rule three: junk food is only for Saturdays.
The first week was hard.
I really missed my chips!
But slowly, I started to feel different.
I had more energy in the morning.
Running felt easier.
Even my skin looked better.
Now Saturday fried chicken tastes even more delicious, because it is special.
Eating smart doesn't mean saying no to yummy food.
It means making good choices most of the time.
Typhoon Day
Last night, the news said a typhoon was coming.
This morning, the sky turned dark gray, and the wind grew strong.
Dad moved the plants inside, and Mom filled some bottles with water.
I helped tape the windows.
By noon, the rain was falling hard.
The trees outside danced left and right in the wind.
We could not go anywhere, so we stayed in the living room together.
Mom made hot noodle soup.
Dad told us stories about the big typhoons when he was young.
My sister and I played cards and listened to the rain.
The power went out for one hour at night, so we lit candles.
It was a little scary but also special.
A typhoon day is not fun for everyone, but staying safe and warm with my family made me feel lucky.
Packing for the Big Trip
Tomorrow, my family is going to Taitung for three days.
Tonight, we are all packing.
This is my first time packing my own backpack, and it is harder than I thought!
At first, I wanted to bring everything: five T-shirts, my games, three books, and my soccer ball.
But my backpack is small.
Mom laughed and said, "We are going for three days, not three months!" So I made a list.
Clothes for three days, a hat, my water bottle, sunscreen, and one book for the train ride.
Dad checked our train tickets on his phone and printed a map of the town.
My sister packed her camera.
She wants to take one hundred photos of the sea.
Now my backpack is light and ready by the door.
I can't sleep.
I keep thinking about the blue sea and the hot spring.
Taitung, here we come!
The Train to Taitung
Our train left the city at nine in the morning.
I love riding trains because you can see so much from the window.
First, we passed tall buildings and busy roads.
Then, little by little, the view changed.
We saw green rice fields, small towns, and long rivers.
After two hours, the best part came: the sea!
The water was so blue that everyone on the train said "Wow!" at the same time.
A grandma sat next to us.
She was going home to Taitung.
She shared some rice cakes with us and told us about the best places to eat there.
"Try the fried rice noodles at the old market," she said.
"My friend has sold them for forty years." We arrived at one thirty.
The air smelled like the sea.
Our vacation finally started, and I already loved Taitung before we left the station.
A Day at the Beach
Today was our beach day in Taitung!
The weather was perfect — sunny with a soft wind.
We put on sunscreen, wore our hats, and walked to the beach after breakfast.
The sand was already warm under our feet.
My sister and I ran into the water first.
The waves pushed us and we laughed and shouted.
Dad tried to surf on a small board, but he fell again and again.
Even the lifeguard laughed!
After lunch, we rested under a big umbrella.
I collected shells with my sister.
She found a white shell that looks like a little fan.
We also built a sandcastle with a bridge and a wall around it.
A big wave came and washed half of it away, but we didn't care.
Before dinner, we watched the sky turn orange and pink.
I took a photo with my heart, not my phone.
I will remember this day forever.
Up the Mountain
On our last day in Taitung, we drove up a mountain to see the sunrise.
We got up at four in the morning!
I was sleepy, but Dad said, "Trust me, it will be worth it." The mountain road had many turns.
When we arrived at the top, the sky was still dark, and the air was cool.
We drank hot milk tea and waited.
Slowly, the sky turned from black to deep blue, then to gold.
Finally, the sun jumped out of the sea of clouds.
The view was so beautiful that nobody said a word.
On the way down, we stopped at a small waterfall and crossed an old bridge.
The water was ice-cold and clear.
We put our feet in and screamed — then laughed.
Dad was right.
Getting up early was hard, but that golden morning was the best part of our whole trip.
The Old Temple Town
Have you ever visited Tainan?
My classmate Emma went there last month, and she can't stop talking about it.
Tainan is one of the oldest cities in Taiwan.
Emma visited a famous temple that is over three hundred years old.
The roof has beautiful dragons, and the doors have paintings of old heroes.
Her grandma taught her how to pray and told her the stories behind the temple.
But Emma's favorite part was the food.
The old streets near the temple are full of small food stands.
She ate shrimp rolls, tofu pudding, and fruit ice.
"Everything was cheap and delicious," she said.
"My stomach was so happy!" Emma took a photo in front of the temple with her grandma.
She keeps it on her desk now.
"A city with old stories feels warm," she says.
I want to visit Tainan this August, too.
Home Sweet Home
Our Taitung trip ended yesterday.
When the train arrived back in our city, it was raining.
We were tired, and our backpacks were heavy with dirty clothes and gifts.
But when we opened the door of our home, something felt wonderful.
"Home sweet home!" Mom said.
My own bed, my own desk, even the old sofa — everything looked friendly, like they were saying, "Welcome back!" At dinner, we looked at our photos and laughed again at Dad's surfing.
My sister chose her best sea photo and set it as the wallpaper on Mom's phone.
I put my little shell on my bookshelf.
Dad asked, "So, where should we go next summer?" Everyone started talking at the same time — the mountains!
An island!
A big city!
We couldn't agree, but it didn't matter.
A trip gives you stories, and home gives you rest.
We are lucky to have both.
Morning Jog with Mom
My mom started jogging three months ago.
Every morning at six, she runs around the river park.
This week, she asked me to join her.
"Six in the morning?
In summer vacation?" I said.
But I said yes.
The first day was terrible.
After five minutes, my legs felt heavy, and I couldn't breathe well.
Mom slowed down for me.
"Don't race," she said.
"Just find your own speed." On the third day, something changed.
My body felt lighter.
I could run for fifteen minutes without stopping.
We saw the morning sun on the river, and old people doing tai chi under the trees.
The world at 6 a.m.
is quiet and beautiful.
Now I understand why Mom loves jogging.
It's not just exercise.
It's the best start to a day.
Tomorrow, we will try to run twenty minutes!
The Basketball Game
Yesterday, our neighborhood had a summer basketball game — kids versus dads!
Everyone came to the school court to watch.
The dads were tall and strong, but we were fast.
In the first half, my friend Jason scored three times, and we led 12 to 8.
The dads looked surprised.
Then they started to play hard.
My dad blocked my shot and laughed, "Sorry, son!" In the last minute, the score was 20 to 20.
Jason passed me the ball.
I jumped and threw it with all my energy.
The ball hit the ring, rolled around...
and dropped in!
We won 22 to 20!
We jumped and shouted like crazy.
The dads bought everyone cold drinks and said, "Good game!
Next month, we want to play again." My arms still hurt today, but I keep smiling when I think about that last ball.
Practice Makes Better
My little sister wants to join the school swimming team in September.
But there is a problem: she is afraid of deep water.
This summer, she goes to the pool three times a week.
Her coach is very patient.
First week: she only practiced kicking with a board.
Second week: she learned to breathe in the water.
Many times she drank the pool water and wanted to cry.
But she never stopped.
Yesterday, something amazing happened.
She swam from one side of the pool to the other side — twenty-five meters — all by herself!
The coach clapped.
Mom almost cried.
My sister climbed out of the pool, tired but smiling like a star.
"How did you do it?" I asked her.
She said, "I was still afraid.
I just practiced one more time every day." I think my little sister just taught me something big.
Ouch! My Knee
Last night, I hurt my knee.
It was my own fault.
My friends called me to play basketball, and I ran to the court right away.
No stretching, no warm-up.
In the first five minutes, I jumped for the ball, landed badly, and fell.
My knee turned red and started to hurt a lot.
My friends helped me walk home.
Dad looked at it carefully and put ice on it.
"It's not too bad," he said, "but you must rest for a few days.
And remember — your body is not a machine.
You have to warm it up." Today, I stayed home with my leg up on a pillow.
My friends sent me funny messages.
Mom made me chicken soup.
Next time, I will spend ten minutes stretching before I play, even if my friends are waiting.
A little warm-up is much better than a week of rest!
A Visit to the Doctor
My cousin Leo got sick this week.
On Monday, he had a headache.
On Tuesday, he had a fever of 38.5 degrees.
His mom took him to see the doctor near their home.
The doctor checked Leo's throat and listened to his heart.
"It's summer flu," the doctor said.
"Many kids have it this month." She gave Leo some medicine and four important rules: take the medicine after meals, drink lots of warm water, sleep more than nine hours, and no ice cream for a week.
"No ice cream?
In summer?" Leo cried.
The doctor laughed, "You can eat it when you are healthy again.
Your body needs rest now, not sugar." Leo followed the rules.
He slept, drank water, and watched cartoons quietly.
Today his fever is gone.
He sent me a message: "I'm back!
Ice cream this Saturday?" Ha!
He is really fine now.
Breathe and Relax
My mom does yoga every evening in the living room.
I always thought it looked boring — just standing and breathing?
Last night, she asked me to try it with her.
I had nothing to do, so I joined.
First, we sat on the floor and closed our eyes.
"Breathe in for four counts, breathe out for four counts," Mom said softly.
Then we did some easy poses.
One was called "the tree." I had to stand on one leg.
I fell twice!
Mom didn't laugh.
She said, "Balance needs practice, like everything else." After thirty minutes, something surprised me.
My body felt warm and soft, and my mind was very quiet.
The little angry feelings from the day were gone.
Mom says exercise is not only about strong muscles.
Sometimes, slow and quiet exercise gives you a different kind of energy.
I think I will join her again tonight.
The Community Race
This morning, our community held a three-kilometer fun race.
Anyone could join — kids, parents, even grandparents.
My whole family signed up.
At seven thirty, about one hundred people stood at the park gate.
The head of our community shouted "Go!" and everyone started running.
Dad ran fast and finished eighth.
Mom and my sister ran together and chatted the whole way.
And me?
At two kilometers, my legs wanted to give up.
An old grandpa, maybe seventy years old, passed me slowly.
He smiled and said, "Young man, don't stop.
Slow is also moving!" I followed him, step by step.
We finished together, and everyone cheered for us.
I didn't win anything, but I finished my first race without walking.
Grandpa gave me a high five at the finish line.
"See you next year," he said.
Yes, next year I will be faster!
The Quiet Library
It was too hot to play outside today, so my friend Mia and I went to the city library.
The library is cool, quiet, and free — the perfect place for a summer afternoon.
We found seats by the big window on the second floor.
Mia read comic books about space.
I picked a mystery story about a missing cat.
The room was so quiet that I could hear the pages turning.
After two hours, we walked around.
The library has a music room, a computer area, and even a small movie room.
A librarian told us about the Summer Reading Game: read ten books, write short notes about them, and win a prize in September.
Mia and I signed up right away.
We borrowed four books each.
Now we have a new plan for the hot days: every Tuesday and Thursday afternoon, you can find us by that big window.
My Favorite Subject
Next month, I will be in eighth grade.
My cousin asked me yesterday, "What is your favorite subject?" I didn't even think for one second: "Science!" Why do I love science?
Because in science class, we don't just read books — we do things.
Last semester, we grew beans in cotton, made a small volcano with baking soda, and used a microscope to look at leaves.
When I saw the tiny green rooms inside a leaf, I couldn't believe my eyes.
A leaf is like a little city!
My science teacher, Mr.
Chen, always says, "Don't just remember the answer.
Ask why." Now I ask "why" about everything.
Why is the sky blue?
Why does ice float?
Why do cats always land on their feet?
Maybe one day I will be a scientist.
But even if I don't, science taught me the most useful skill: staying curious about the world.
The New Classmate
Last April, a new student came to our class.
His name is Ryo, and he moved from Japan because of his dad's job.
On his first day, he was very shy.
He knew some Chinese, but he was afraid to speak.
At lunch time, Ryo sat alone.
I remembered my first day at a new school — that lonely feeling.
So I took my lunch box and sat next to him.
"Hi, I'm Ting.
Do you like baseball?" His eyes lit up.
"Yes!
I love the Rakuten Monkeys!" That was the beginning.
Now Ryo is one of my best friends.
He taught me some Japanese words, and I help him with Chinese homework.
He is not shy anymore — actually, he is the funniest one in our group.
Sometimes a friendship starts with one small hello.
I'm glad I said it first.
Study Buddies
In two weeks, there is a big test for the new semester.
My classmate Amber and I made a plan: we study together every morning from nine to eleven.
We call ourselves "study buddies." Our rules are simple.
Phones stay in the schoolbag.
We study for twenty-five minutes, then rest for five minutes.
In the rest time, we eat a little snack or just look at the trees outside.
Studying together works like magic.
When I don't understand a math question, Amber explains it to me.
When she forgets an English word, I act it out and make her laugh.
Yesterday, I acted out the word "chicken" — she laughed for five minutes!
Alone, I always want to give up after half an hour.
Together, two hours pass quickly.
A good study buddy doesn't just make you smarter.
She makes learning feel less lonely.
The Little Stationery Shop
Near my school, there is a little stationery shop.
The owner is an old man we all call Uncle Wang.
His shop is small and a little messy, but it has everything: notebooks, erasers, rulers, scissors, glue, and hundreds of pens.
Today, Mom gave me two hundred dollars to buy things for the new semester.
At the shop, I picked three notebooks, a blue pen, and a new eraser.
Uncle Wang looked at my eraser and laughed, "You bought the same one in March.
Do you eat erasers?" I laughed too.
I always lose them!
When I paid, Uncle Wang gave me a small gift — a sticker of a cat reading a book.
"For hard-working students," he said with a wink.
Big stores are cheaper, and online shopping is easy.
But I still love Uncle Wang's little shop.
Some places sell things; his shop gives warm feelings, too.
Choosing a Club
Next semester, every student in my grade must join one club.
There are so many choices: the music club, the dance club, the science club, the cooking club, and more.
I couldn't decide, so I asked my friends.
Jason said, "Join the basketball club with me!
We can practice together." Mia said, "The art club is the best.
The teacher is so kind." My sister said, "Cooking club!
Then you can make me cookies." Ha!
Everyone had a different answer.
Last night, I made a list of things I love: music, drawing, and eating cookies (making them sounds hard).
Then I remembered something — my neighbor's brother plays the guitar, and every time I hear it, I stop and listen.
My heart already knew the answer.
This morning, I wrote my choice on the form: the guitar club.
I can't wait for September!
Best Friends Fight Too
Kevin and I have been best friends for six years.
But last week, we had a big fight.
It started with a small thing.
I told Kevin a secret about my dream — I want to be a singer.
Two days later, another classmate asked me, "So you want to be a singer?" I was so angry.
Kevin broke his promise!
For three days, we didn't talk.
It felt terrible.
Playing games alone was boring.
Lunch tasted bad.
On the fourth day, Kevin came to my house with a drink in his hand.
"I'm sorry," he said.
"I was wrong.
I told Ben because I was proud of you.
But a secret is a secret.
Please forgive me." I took the drink and said, "Next time, just cheer for me quietly." We both laughed.
A real friendship is not about never fighting.
It's about saying sorry, forgiving, and still choosing each other after the fight.
Grandma's First Tablet
Last week, my uncle bought Grandma a tablet for her seventieth birthday.
"It's too hard for me," Grandma said.
"I'm too old for these things." But we didn't give up.
Every afternoon this week, I became Grandma's little teacher.
Day one: how to turn it on and make the words bigger.
Day two: how to take photos.
She took thirty photos of her flowers!
Day three: video calls.
When Uncle's face appeared on the screen, Grandma laughed like a young girl.
"I can see you!
Can you see me?" she shouted.
She didn't need to shout, but it was so cute.
Now Grandma uses her tablet every day.
She watches cooking videos, looks at our family photos, and video calls her sister in Kaohsiung every night.
"I was wrong," Grandma told me yesterday.
"You are never too old to learn something new." I'm so proud of my student!
The Day the Wi-Fi Died
Yesterday at noon, the internet at our home stopped working.
No videos, no online games, no music.
My sister and I looked at each other.
"What do we do now?" she asked.
Dad called the internet company.
They said, "We can fix it tomorrow morning." Tomorrow?!
A whole day without Wi-Fi?
At first, we walked around the house like two lost cats.
Then Mom took out an old box.
Inside, there were board games, cards, and puzzles from years ago.
We played a card game called Big Two.
My sister won three times and danced around the sofa.
After dinner, we did a five-hundred-piece puzzle of a night sky and chatted about everything — school, funny dreams, our next trip.
We didn't finish the puzzle, but nobody wanted to stop.
The Wi-Fi came back this morning.
I'm happy about that.
But you know what?
Last night was the most fun night of this summer.
A Message to the Wrong Person
My classmate Nina told me a funny and scary story about her weekend.
On Saturday, Nina wanted to send a message to her best friend Emma.
She typed: "Math homework is so boring!
Teacher Lin gives too much homework.
I want to sleep in class!" Then she pressed send.
One second later, her face turned white.
She didn't send it to Emma.
She sent it to...
Teacher Lin!
Their names start with the same letter, and she picked the wrong name.
Nina wanted to hide under her bed forever.
But ten minutes later, Teacher Lin replied: "Ha ha, I know it's a lot.
But the test is coming.
Sleep early tonight, and you won't want to sleep in class.
😊" Nina says she learned two things.
One: Teacher Lin is much kinder than she thought.
Two: always check the name twice before you press send!
Movie Night at Home
Every Friday night is movie night in our family.
We don't go to the theater.
We make our own theater at home!
Here is how we do it.
First, we vote for the movie.
This week, my sister and I wanted an animal cartoon, and Dad wanted a space movie.
Mom had the last vote...
and she chose the cartoon.
Dad said, "Next week, space.
You promised!" Then we prepare the room.
We turn off all the lights, put big pillows on the floor, and Mom makes a mountain of popcorn.
Dad always adds too much butter, but nobody says no.
The movie was about a penguin who couldn't swim.
We laughed, and near the end, Mom cried a little.
(She always cries in movies!) A theater ticket costs money, but our movie night is free — and it has the best seats, the best snacks, and the best people in the world.
One More Level
"One more level, then I'll stop." I said this at eight o'clock.
Then at nine.
Then at ten.
When Mom knocked on my door at ten thirty, I was still playing.
The game was so exciting.
My character finally got the fire sword, and my team needed me.
But Mom sat down next to me and asked one simple question: "Are you controlling the game, or is the game controlling you?" I wanted to say "I'm controlling it," but then I looked at the clock.
Three and a half hours passed, and it felt like thirty minutes.
My eyes were dry.
My homework wasn't done.
Hmm.
Maybe the game was winning — not just the level, but me.
So we made a deal: on game days, I set an alarm for ninety minutes.
When it rings, I finish and stand up.
It has been four days, and the alarm works.
The fire sword is still there tomorrow.
My time is not.
The Stranger Online
Last month, my cousin Ella got a message in her game app.
It said: "Hi!
You play so well!
I'm Amy, 13, from Taichung.
Let's be friends!" Ella was happy to have a new friend.
They chatted about games and music every day.
Then "Amy" started asking strange questions.
"Which school do you go to?
Send me a photo!
What is your address?
I want to send you a gift." Ella felt something was wrong.
Why does a new friend need her address?
Ella told her mom.
Her mom said, "Good job telling me.
On the internet, you can't see who is really behind the screen.
A person who says they are 13 may not be 13." Together, they blocked and reported the account.
The game company later removed it — it was a fake account, and "Amy" wasn't a kid at all.
Ella still plays games and makes online friends.
But now she has a golden rule: real friends don't need your private information.
A Day Without Screens
Yesterday, our family tried a challenge: one whole day without screens.
No phones, no TV, no computers — from morning to night.
Dad put all our devices in a basket on top of the fridge.
The morning was the hardest part.
My hand kept looking for my phone, like a habit.
My sister touched the empty table where the tablet usually sits and sighed.
But slowly, the day filled up by itself.
We made pancakes and ate them slowly.
I finished a whole comic book.
In the afternoon, we rode bikes to the river and flew a kite.
My sister taught our dog to give a high five — it took her two hours, and it worked!
At night, we sat on the balcony, ate watermelon, and counted stars.
Dad told us about his childhood without smartphones.
"We were never bored," he said.
"The world was our screen." One day was enough for me to see it: screens are fun, but they eat time quietly.
Now I want a screen-free day every month.
The Forest Walk
This morning, Dad took my sister and me to a forest trail in the mountains.
"Today, no music, no phones," he said.
"Let's use our ears and eyes." The forest was cool and quiet — but not really quiet.
When we stopped talking, we heard everything: birds singing high in the trees, a stream running somewhere below, and the wind moving through the leaves like a soft song.
We played a game: who can find the most living things?
My sister found a line of ants carrying a big leaf.
I found a spider web with rain drops on it, shining like a necklace.
Dad won — he found a green snake sleeping on a branch!
We watched it quietly from far away and let it sleep.
After two hours, we walked out of the forest.
My legs were tired, but my head felt clean and fresh.
The forest is like a big green home, and we were lucky visitors.
Monkeys on the Mountain
Last Sunday, we hiked a mountain in Kaohsiung.
It is famous for one thing: monkeys.
Before we started, a sign said in big letters: "Do not feed the monkeys.
Keep food in your bags!" On the trail, we saw monkeys everywhere — on trees, on rocks, even on the handrail.
A baby monkey rode on its mother's back.
It was so cute that everyone stopped to watch.
Then, a funny but scary thing happened.
A man in front of us took out a bag of bread.
In one second, a big monkey jumped down, grabbed the whole bag, and climbed up a tree!
The man stood there with his mouth open.
The monkey ate the bread and looked at him, like it was saying, "Thanks for lunch!" A park worker told us, "When people feed monkeys, the monkeys stop finding food in nature.
Then they take food from people.
It's bad for them and for us." Now I understand: loving wild animals means keeping a good distance.
The Firefly Night
My aunt lives in a small village near the mountains.
She called us last week: "The fireflies are dancing these days.
Come and see!" So last night, we drove to her village.
After dinner, Aunt gave us a rule: "No flashlights, no phone lights.
Fireflies talk to each other with light.
Our lights confuse them." We walked slowly on the dark path beside the stream, holding hands.
Then we saw them.
First one, then ten, then hundreds — tiny yellow-green lights floating in the dark, like stars falling into the grass.
My sister whispered, "It's magic." Nobody wanted to talk loudly.
Aunt told us fireflies only live in clean places.
"Twenty years ago, this stream was dirty, and the fireflies disappeared.
The village worked together to clean it, and after many years, they came back." On the way home, I thought: the fireflies didn't just come back by themselves.
People brought them back with care.
That little light is a big lesson.
The Sea Turtle's Trash Dinner
Yesterday, I watched an ocean program with my family.
It was about sea turtles, and one part made me almost cry.
A sea turtle was sick on a beach.
Doctors helped it and found the problem: there was plastic inside its stomach — a plastic bag, a straw, and pieces of a bottle.
To a turtle, a plastic bag in the water looks just like a jellyfish, its favorite food.
It can't tell the difference.
The good news?
After two months of care, the turtle got healthy, and the team sent it back to the sea.
Everyone on the beach clapped as it swam away.
The program said: every year, tons of plastic go into the ocean.
But it also showed hope.
Some beaches are now cleaned by volunteers every month, and more people bring their own bags and bottles.
My sister and I made a promise last night: no more plastic straws for us.
It is a small thing.
But if a million kids do one small thing, that is a big thing.
Beach Cleanup Day
This morning, my family joined a beach cleanup near the harbor.
About fifty people came — students, families, and even a grandpa with his dog.
The leader gave us gloves and bags and said, "Pick up trash, but leave the shells and crabs.
They live here; we are just helpers." In two hours, my bag was full.
I picked up bottles, a broken toy, plastic bags, and so many straws.
My sister found a shoe!
The strangest thing was a TV remote.
How did a remote get to the beach?
The sea holds many strange stories.
At the end, we put all the bags together — thirty-two big bags of trash from one small beach.
The leader said, "Look at this mountain of trash.
It didn't walk here by itself.
And it won't leave by itself either." My arms hurt, and my shoes are full of sand.
But when I looked back at the clean beach, with little crabs running near the water, I felt something warm.
We gave the beach back to them, at least for today.
Watching the Stars
Last night, we stayed at Grandpa's house in the countryside.
After dinner, Grandpa turned off the yard lights and put three chairs on the grass.
"Tonight's TV program," he smiled and pointed at the sky, "is up there." I looked up and couldn't say a word.
The sky was full of stars — hundreds, maybe thousands.
In the city, I usually see five or six stars.
Here, the sky looked like someone spilled a box of diamonds.
Grandpa knows the stars well.
He showed us a group of stars that looks like a spoon.
"Sailors used the stars as their map at night," he said.
We also saw one star that moved fast in a straight line.
"That's not a star," Grandpa laughed.
"That's a satellite — a machine people put in the sky." We lay on the grass until midnight.
I made a wish on the brightest star.
I won't tell you my wish, but I will tell you this: the best screen in the world doesn't need Wi-Fi.
A Day on Uncle's Farm
My uncle is a farmer.
He has a small farm with rice fields, ten cows, and many chickens.
Today, my sister and I were his little helpers for one day.
Our first job was at six in the morning: feeding the chickens.
The chickens ran to us like crazy fans at a concert!
Next, we helped Uncle move fresh grass for the cows.
A brown cow licked my hand.
Her tongue was rough and warm, and I screamed — then laughed.
At noon, Aunt cooked lunch with vegetables from the farm.
Rice, eggs, and soup — everything was fresh.
"City kids think rice comes from the supermarket," Uncle joked.
"Now you know it comes from months of hard work." In the afternoon, we walked along the green fields and caught grasshoppers.
Before we left, Uncle gave us a box of eggs.
"Wages for my workers," he said.
Farming is hard work — my back still hurts.
But now, every bowl of rice looks different to me.
Thank you, farmers!
A Rainy Day at the Museum
It rained hard this morning, so our plan for the water park died.
"Let's try the city museum," Mom said.
"It's free on Wednesdays." My sister and I were not excited.
A museum?
On our vacation?
We were so wrong.
The museum had a special show about dinosaurs this month.
A T-Rex skeleton stood in the main hall, taller than a bus!
There was also a room where you could touch real rocks from a volcano, and a dark room that showed the night sky on the ceiling.
My favorite part was the "old street" area.
It showed our city one hundred years ago — old shops, old buses, and photos of people from the past.
Mom found a photo of the street where our home is now.
It was a rice field back then!
We stayed until the museum closed.
On the bus home, my sister asked, "Can we come back next Wednesday?" Rainy days are not so bad after all.
My First Solo Ride
Yesterday, I did something for the first time: I took the subway across the city alone, to my grandma's place.
Mom helped me make a plan first.
Take the red line for six stops, change to the blue line at the main station, then ride three more stops.
She sent Grandma a message: "He is leaving now.
Green T-shirt, blue backpack." The main station was crowded and noisy.
People walked fast, like rivers going in every direction.
For one minute, I couldn't find the blue line, and my heart beat fast.
Then I remembered Mom's words: "Don't panic.
Look for the signs above." I found the blue arrow, followed it, and got on the right train.
When I walked out of the station, Grandma was waiting with a smile and a cold drink.
She called Mom: "Our little man arrived — all by himself!" On the train, I was a little scared.
Now I feel one year older.
The city is big, but I am bigger than yesterday.
Shopping for the New Semester
School starts next week, so Mom took us shopping today.
But this time, there was a new rule: my sister and I each got five hundred dollars, and we had to plan our own shopping.
I made a list first: a notebook (I checked the price last week — fifty dollars), two pens, white socks, and a new water bottle.
My old bottle smells like old tea.
Yuck.
At the store, I saw a cool pencil case with a basketball design.
Three hundred dollars!
If I bought it, I couldn't buy the water bottle.
I stood there for five minutes.
Want or need?
Finally, I put it back.
My old pencil case still works fine.
At the counter, I paid and got twenty dollars back.
My sister spent every dollar — but she forgot the socks!
Mom smiled and said, "Now you know why I always make a list." Shopping with your own money teaches you fast.
The Store That Never Sleeps
Last night, my dog Lucky got sick at eleven o'clock.
The animal hospital told us what to buy, and there was only one place open: the convenience store on the corner.
Walking there with Dad at midnight, I saw a different city.
The streets were quiet and dark, but the store shone like a little sun.
Inside, a worker was making coffee for a taxi driver.
A nurse in uniform was buying dinner — her workday just ended at midnight!
We got what we needed, and Dad also bought hot soup.
At the counter, we paid, sent a package, and Dad even printed a paper for work — all in one small store, in three minutes.
On the way home, Dad said, "When I was young, everything closed at nine.
Life now is so convenient.
But remember, convenient means many people are working while we sleep." Lucky is fine today.
And I have a new habit: I always say thank you to the night workers of our city.
What Do You Want to Be?
Our summer homework has a special task: interview three adults about their jobs.
This week, I finished all three interviews.
First, I asked my aunt, the computer engineer.
"I build apps that help people," she said.
"The best part?
When a problem finally works out at 2 a.m., I feel like a hero." She laughed, "The worst part is also 2 a.m." Next was Mr.
Lin, the chef at the restaurant near us.
He showed me his hands — full of small burn marks.
"Every mark is a lesson," he said.
"I feed people.
Tired hands, happy hearts." Last, I interviewed a police officer at the station by our school.
She said the job is sometimes dangerous, but she loves helping people feel safe.
Three people, three different jobs, one same thing: they all light up when they talk about helping others.
Maybe that's the secret.
I still don't know what I want to be.
But now I know what kind of person I want to be.
A Letter to My Future Self
Today, our teacher gave us a special pre-semester task online: write a letter to yourself, and open it on the last day of ninth grade — two years from now.
Here is part of my letter: "Dear Future Me, how are you?
Right now, I am sitting at my desk on the last weekend of summer vacation.
This summer, I read every day, learned to cook fried rice, swam 25 meters, and cleaned a beach.
I feel taller inside.
Do you still play basketball with Dad?
Is Lucky still stealing socks?
Did you keep your promise about the plastic straws?
My goals for you: pass 25 meters — no, 100 meters — in swimming.
Read fifty more books.
Be brave and sing on the stage once.
And please, be nicer to our little sister.
She is annoying but she is also our best fan.
I believe in you.
Everything is possible.
From, Summer Me, 2026." I sealed the letter in an envelope.
See you in two years, future me!
Ready for Tomorrow
Tomorrow is the first day of the new semester.
Tonight, my room looks like a little train station — everything is moving!
My uniform is washed and hanging on the door.
My schoolbag is packed: new notebooks, pens, my water bottle, and my library card.
I checked my class schedule three times.
Math on Monday morning...
okay, not a perfect start, but fine.
At dinner, we talked about our summer.
Mom asked, "What was the best part?" My sister said the beach.
Dad said the family race.
I couldn't choose one.
The morning jogs?
The fireflies?
Cooking with Mom?
The whole summer was like a book full of good stories.
Am I nervous about tomorrow?
A little.
New classroom, new teachers, maybe new classmates.
But I am more excited than nervous.
I did so many new things this summer — one more new thing is nothing!
Good night, summer.
See you next year.
Tomorrow, here I come.
